NEW DELHI: Shiromani Akali Dal , one of the BJP 's oldest allies, on Tuesday rejoined the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) ahead of the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections , six years after the two parties parted ways over the contentious farm laws.Union home minister Amit Shah announced that the BJP and the SAD would contest all 117 assembly seats in Punjab together, with hinting that chief minister's post going to the "big brother" Akali Dal.Addressing a joint presser in New Delhi, Shah welcomed the Sukhbir Singh Badal-led party back into the NDA and said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had described the development by saying that the "NDA is now complete".Shah described the Akali Dal as the BJP's "oldest ally" and said the relationship between the two parties went back to the Atal Bihari Vajpayee-LK Advani era."Our relationship with Akali Dal has always been strong, our ties go back to Vajpayee-Advani era," he said."From today onwards, the Akali Dal will work in politics as an officially recognised ally of the NDA. As the entire country is celebrating Guru Parv, it is a matter of great joy for all NDA alliance partners that the Akali Dal, one of the NDA's oldest allies, is returning to the NDA once again… Prime Minister also spoke to Sukhbir Ji and the President with great joy over the phone. He expressed the sentiment that the NDA is now complete," Shah said.The reunion comes six years after the SAD walked out of the NDA in 2020 over the three farm laws introduced by the Centre, which had triggered widespread protests by farmers.Notably, Prime Minister Narendra Modi had announced the repeal of the three farm laws on Gurpurab, November 19, 2021. The two parties have now reunited on the occasion of Gurpurab, which falls on November 24 this year.Shah said the alliance would announce several key points in its manifesto, but set out its priorities at the outset. "BJP, the Akali Dal, and the NDA will contest in Punjab, and we will announce several key points in our manifesto. But, I want to make one thing very clear: eliminating drugs from Punjab will be our primary goal, eliminating corruption in Punjab will be our primary goal, and strengthening nationalist forces in Punjab will also be our primary goal. The current government in the state, led by Kejriwal Ji, had come to power promising to eliminate drugs within three months. They promised to eliminate drugs, but the problem has not been eradicated; it has increased. In 2017, Rahul Gandhi Ji had promised that drugs would be eliminated within one term. He made that promise, but his party also did nothing to address the drug problem. Now, I want to reiterate a promise that I made there: by December 31, 2029, we will make Punjab completely drug-free."BJP national president Nitin Nabin said seat-sharing arrangements would be discussed later. "We will discuss seat-sharing arrangements in detail later, but today, by coming together, we are clearly conveying the message that we have united to serve Punjab. In the coming days, under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi Ji, we will continue our commitment to Punjab's development, just as we have always prioritised development and good governance. We will take the benefits of development to the last person in society," he said.Nabin also called the occasion a significant one. "Today is a very sacred day, and on this occasion, such a significant decision is being taken in the interest of Punjab and the country. I come from the city of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, and on this occasion of Prakash Parv, I believe the light of development, justice, and good governance will spread across Punjab. I extend my heartfelt wishes to Sukhbir Badal and to all the members of his party and to all the people of Punjab. Your joining the NDA alliance will strengthen all of us. I also believe that this alliance between the Shiromani Akali Dal and our party is a natural alliance, a natural partnership," he said.SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal, who spoke at the meeting with Shah and Nabin on Tuesday, described the tie with the BJP as one that goes beyond electoral politics. "This is not just a political alliance. There is an emotional bond. As my late father used to say, Akali Dal-BJP is an inseparable, deeply bonded relationship," he said.Badal said the alliance had been formed for the larger good and credited it with contributing to peace in the state. "This is an alliance for the interest of Punjab, for the interest of the country and for the interest of the Sikh community. You must have seen how long this alliance lasted and how many governments were formed; Punjab is progressing. There has been peace in Punjab. There has been brotherhood in Punjab," he said.He also underlined the historical role of his party. "Shiromani Akali Dal is not a new party. It is the second oldest party in the history of India. The leadership of Shiromani Akali Dal and the workers made the biggest contribution to the independence of the country. Even after independence, be it the issue of the poor, be it the issue of Punjab, be it the issue of labourers, be it the issue of the nation, Shiromani Akali Dal struggled," he said.The two parties are among the longest-standing allies in Indian politics, and have historically been partners in Punjab. The Akali Dal walked out of the alliance in 2020 over the Union government's intention to introduce the three farm laws, which triggered widespread protests by farmers. The laws were later withdrawn, but the two parties contested the 2022 Assembly elections separately.Their electoral record shows how much the split, and the years around it, cost them. The SAD won 48 seats in 2007 and 56 in 2012, its strongest performance, while the BJP won 19 and 12 respectively. Together, the two parties secured 67 seats in 2007 and 68 in 2012.The numbers fell sharply in the elections that followed. In 2017, the SAD's tally dropped to 15 seats and the BJP's to three, while the Congress won 77 and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) 20. In 2022, the SAD won just three seats and the BJP two. The Congress fell to 18, while the AAP registered a victory with 92 seats.Measured against its earlier record, the SAD's 2022 tally was 45 seats lower than in 2007 and 53 lower than in 2012, a decline of 93.75 per cent and 94.64 per cent respectively. The BJP's strength fell by 17 seats, or 89.47 per cent, from its 2007 tally, and by 10 seats, or 83.33 per cent, from its 2012 tally.
Article Summary: BJP welcomes back 'oldest ally' Akali Dal ahead of Punjab polls in 2027. Union home minister Amit Shah announced that the BJP and the SAD would contest all 117 assembly seats in Punjab together. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the development by saying that the "NDA is now complete"

NEW DELHI: AIMIM Bihar chief Akhtarul Iman on Monday defended his controversial remarks comparing the way brides are dressed and presented at wedding receptions to a "tawaif", saying his comments were rooted in Islamic teachings and intended only for Muslims who wish to follow the religion."Tawaifs have more shame than your bahus," Iman said at a gathering.Iman's remarks, made at a public gathering (jalsa), have drawn criticism from political leaders across party lines. He had objected to the practice of dressing brides in traditional finery (solah shringar) and seating them at receptions for relatives and friends to see, arguing that Muslim women should observe 'purdah'.Responding to the criticism, Iman said observing the veil was obligatory (farz) in Islam and that his remarks reflected the teachings of Islamic religious scholars."India has a long tradition of Sufi saints and respect for women. Wearing sindoor is a matter of religious faith, and similarly, Islam requires women to observe purdah and wear hijab. No one should disrespect a religious scholar’s cap or tear a woman’s hijab. My comments were intended only for Muslims who wish to follow Islamic teachings, particularly regarding modesty and interactions between men and women," he told news agency ANI.His remarks triggered sharp reactions from political leaders, with several questioning his views on women's autonomy and the portrayal of women at weddings. Samajwadi Party MP Shiv Pal Singh Patel said the money given to brides at weddings was a form of blessing and that the practice was not limited to any one religion."The money given at weddings is essentially a form of blessing for the daughter; this is a practice found across all religions... The comparison involving Jamila and Sita touches upon the issue of women’s autonomy. It is not as if there is any indecent exposure; if a woman’s face is uncovered and she is adorned, what is wrong with that?.. The regressive notion that a woman must always remain completely covered is something that should not exist. .. I believe people, including our Muslim brothers, should oppose such thinking," he said.Congress leader Mumtaz Patel also condemned Iman's remarks, saying they were derogatory towards women and did not reflect Islamic teachings."It is very, very disgusting to see the so-called representatives of the community, especially coming from a party like the AIMIM that is supposedly representing Muslims, talk so derogatorily about women. Nowhere does Islam demean women like that. The religion or the culture does not treat women this way. There is a whole narrative being spread where statements like these make Islam a very easy target for everyone to condemn. I condemn this statement, and being a Muslim woman, I think it is absolutely, absolutely wrong..." she said.Uttar Pradesh cabinet minister Om Prakash Rajbhar said different religions had different traditions, but accused leaders like Iman of promoting hatred instead of focusing on issues such as education, healthcare and employment."Different religions have different traditions. These people always talk about hatred. We never hear anyone say, at the very least, that we should talk about educating society, education, health, employment, jobs, peace and brotherhood. Why don't these people talk about these things? They spread this venom in society and conspire to defame it," he said.BJP leader Danish Iqbal also criticised Iman, accusing religious conservatives of trying to impose restrictions on Muslim women's lives in the name of Sharia. He said the Constitution had enabled women to pursue careers across different fields."In this country, regressive maulanas (clerics) have made numerous attempts to impose restrictions on the lives of Muslim women in the name of Sharia. They have sought to enslave them—effectively trying to extinguish their very lives. However, the Constitution of India has empowered Muslim women to such an extent that they are now becoming pilots, doctors, and boxers, excelling across various fields. Despite the persistent efforts of these maulanas—who have consistently used the fear of Sharia to exert control—the Constitution of India has paved the way for Muslim women to reach the pinnacle of success," he said.
Article Summary: AIMIM Bihar chief Akhtarul Iman defended his controversial remarks comparing the way brides are dressed and presented at wedding receptions to a "tawaif" He said his comments were rooted in Islamic teachings and intended only for Muslims who wish to follow the religion. His remarks have drawn criticism from political leaders across party lines.

NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) leader Ram Gopal Yadav on Tuesday confirmed that his party has proposed 26 seats to the Congress for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections, as the two INDIA bloc allies held their second round of seat-sharing discussions in New Delhi.Yadav said the party had identified 20 seats where the SP had secured between 60,000 and 70,000 votes in the previous election, while the Congress had received around 2,000 votes.When asked about the SP proposing 26 seats to the Congress, Yadav told reporters, “Yes, we have proposed… 20 such seats have been proposed where we got 60-70 thousand votes and they got 2 thousand.”He added that the proposed seats would be discussed in detail during the second day of deliberations.The talks come as both parties seek to finalise a seat-sharing arrangement for the 403-member Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections scheduled for 2027. The first round of formal discussions was held on Monday at the Delhi residence of senior Congress MP Pramod Tiwari, with leaders from both sides expressing confidence that an agreement could be reached.Congress MP Imran Masood said on Tuesday that the negotiations were guided by mutual cooperation rather than rigid demands.“There is a difference between 'demanding' seats and 'cooperating '. Article Title: India's health bill: Who really pays?
Article Text:
AI generated image

The hospital-building spend

Excluding capital investments, households still pay a larger share of day-to-day healthcare costs.

What changed over the decade?

By 2023–24, government spending had overtaken direct household payments.

One country, very different health bills

What happens when you walk into a hospital?

Medicines bought separately account for over 42% of what Indian households pay directly for healthcare.

Who ultimately pays?

In October 2026, a 27-year-old woman from Mathura who had lost the ability to walk underwent two complex spinal operations in Lucknow. At a private hospital, doctors estimated, the treatment could have cost Rs 6–7 lakh. Under Ayushman Bharat, she received it free, TOI reported That same month, in Odisha's Bargarh district, a daily-wage worker was borrowing money to buy medicines for his family. His son's chemotherapy was covered under Ayushman Bharat, but as TOI reported , the family's monthly medicine requirements alone amounted to Rs 20,000.Both stories point to the same reality, albeit with different outcomes. The government is now picking up a larger share of the country's health bill, yet on the ground, massive medical costs can still push individual households into financial distress.Imagine India's entire healthcare bill as Rs 100. In 2013–14, families paid Rs 64.20 directly from their pockets, the government spent Rs 28.60, and other sources financed the remaining Rs 7.20.By 2023–24, the government's share had risen to Rs 43.50, while direct household payments accounted for Rs 42.70. Other financing arrangements, including private insurance, accounted for the remaining Rs 13.80. In absolute terms, government health expenditure rose from Rs 1.30 lakh crore in 2013–14 to Rs 4.14 lakh crore in 2023–24.Direct household payments increased much more slowly, from Rs 2.91 lakh crore to Rs 4.06 lakh crore. Government spending thus exceeded direct household payments by around Rs 8,000 crore.Government expenditure first overtook direct household payments in the National Health Accounts series in 2021–22, when pandemic-related spending pushed its share to 48%. A closer look at the latest National Health Accounts reveals what lies behind these numbers.Of the Rs 4.14 lakh crore spent by the government in 2023–24, approximately Rs 1.13 lakh crore was capital expenditure on healthcare infrastructure, equipment and other long-term investments. Excluding that, government spending on current healthcare, which is the money used to provide services and goods during the year, stood at about Rs 3.01 lakh crore. Households, meanwhile, paid Rs 4.06 lakh crore directly.For every Rs 100 spent on current healthcare services and goods, the government accounted for Rs 36, while households paid Rs 48.50 directly. Other sources financed the remaining Rs 15.50.However, government spending on current healthcare also more than tripled, from about Rs 98,000 crore in 2013–14 to Rs 3.01 lakh crore in 2023–24. The government's share of current healthcare expenditure rose from 23.2% to 36%.Nearly half the decade-long decline in the household share of total healthcare spending occurred in a single year, when it fell from 58.7% to 48.8% in 2017–18. This coincided with a change in the survey used to estimate household health expenditure and preceded the September 2018 launch of PM-JAY. How much of the decline was attributable to the change in estimation remains unclear.Government health expenditure increased by approximately 219% over the decade, without adjusting for inflation. Direct household payments grew by about 40%. For every Rs 100 the government spent on health in 2013–14, it was spending about Rs 319 a decade later. For households, Rs 100 became about Rs 140.Ayushman Bharat, launched in 2018, has been a prominent initiative in this expansion. Its hospital insurance component, the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), provides eligible families with annual health cover of up to Rs 5 lakh for specified hospital treatments. In October 2024, eligibility was extended to all senior citizens aged 70 and above, irrespective of their economic status. But India's increased public spending goes well beyond hospital insurance.Government-financed health insurance schemes, including PM-JAY and state-specific schemes, accounted for Rs 33,385 crore in 2023–24, or about 8% of government health expenditure. A much larger part of public spending supports the healthcare system itself. Government spending on primary healthcare, the first point of contact for many patients, increased from about Rs 50,000 crore in 2013–14 to Rs 1.53 lakh crore in 2023–24. It accounted for roughly half of the government's current health expenditure in 2023–24.Through the National Health Mission and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, the government has sought to expand basic consultations, maternal and childcare services, access to essential medicines and diagnostic tests. State and local governments accounted for nearly 68% of government health expenditure in 2023–24, underscoring their role in this expansion.In 2023–24, government expenditure exceeded direct household payments in 13 of the 21 states and UTs for which the National Health Accounts provided comparable estimates. In the other eight, families still paid more directly. In Uttarakhand, the government accounted for 66% of total healthcare expenditure, whereas households paid 26.7% directly. The government's share stood at 57.9% in Odisha and 59.5% in Assam.Kerala shows the opposite pattern. For every Rs 100 spent on healthcare in the state, households contributed Rs 65.20 directly, against Rs 25 from the government. In West Bengal, the figures were Rs 63 and Rs 30. State-level government expenditure figures include spending by the Union government and local bodies, not merely the state government's own health budget. The estimates for household spending are based on survey data from 2017–18, updated for subsequent years.The 2025 National Sample Survey indicated that health insurance or healthcare financing coverage has risen from fewer than one in five Indians in 2017–18 to nearly half, largely through government-sponsored schemes.At least half of outpatient treatment episodes at public facilities involved no direct medical expenditure. Average out-of-pocket medical expenditure per hospitalisation, excluding childbirth, was Rs 6,631 at public facilities against Rs 50,508 at private hospitals. While the types of treatment may differ, private hospitals, including those empanelled under government schemes, accounted for 60.3% of hospitalisations excluding childbirth.Medicines remain a major financial burden, with households spending Rs 1.71 lakh crore on separately purchased medicines in 2023–24, accounting for roughly 42% of their direct healthcare expenditure. While PM-JAY primarily covers hospitalisation, initiatives such as government free-drug programmes and Jan Aushadhi seek to reduce everyday medical costs. The number of Jan Aushadhi outlets rose from around 80 in 2014 to around 11,000 by March 2024.Families also finance healthcare through insurance premiums. Expenditure through private health insurance, which includes employer-based group cover and individual policies, rose from 3.4% of total health expenditure in 2013–14 to 10.2% in 2023–24. When we look at where healthcare funds originate, including household insurance contributions, the picture changes. Households supplied Rs 55.70 of every Rs 100 spent on current healthcare in 2023–24, down from Rs 72.90 in 2013–14. The contribution from government budgets and grants rose from Rs 21.10 to Rs 34 over the same period.There is also a cost that the National Health Accounts cannot capture: the treatment someone needed but could not afford. A patient treated free at a government hospital and someone who forgoes treatment because it is unaffordable can both record zero direct medical expenditure. Their experiences could hardly be more different. The real measure of India's healthcare progress is whether an Indian can afford to fall ill without becoming poor.
Article Summary: Medicines bought separately account for over 42% of what Indian households pay directly for healthcare. The government is now picking up a larger share of the country's health bill, yet massive medical costs can still push individual households into financial distress. Government health expenditure increased by approximately 219% over the decade, without adjusting for inflation.

NEW DELHI: India and Nepal on Monday signed eight agreements to expand cooperation in sectors including space technology, security, healthcare, agriculture and sustainable urban development, following talks between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah in New Delhi.The two leaders also virtually flagged off the Saryu-Kamala Express, connecting Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh with Janakpur in Nepal, and jointly inaugurated several development projects during Balen Shah’s two-day state visit to India.At a joint press conference after the talks, Modi said the two countries had taken several important decisions to strengthen bilateral relations.“I am very pleased to welcome Balendra Shah ji to India on his first bilateral visit after becoming the Prime Minister of Nepal. A few months ago, when he addressed the United Nations as the world’s youngest Prime Minister, we got a clear glimpse of his vision. Over the past few hours of our discussions, I have sensed his clear vision and commitment towards Nepal’s future and India-Nepal relations. The historic mandate given to him by the people of Nepal this year reflects the aspirations and hopes of the country’s younger generation. India has always been a partner in the development journey of a strong and prosperous Nepal.In this spirit, today we have taken several important decisions to take our relations to new heights,” PM Modi said.The prime minister also announced a development cooperation package of 24,000 crore Nepali rupees (approximately Rs 15,000 crore) to support Nepal’s reconstruction and long-term development, particularly in the wake of the devastating floods in August.“We express our deep condolences for the loss of lives caused by the devastating floods in Nepal in August. Today, we announce a development cooperation package of 24,000 crore Nepali rupees to give fresh impetus to Nepal’s reconstruction and long-term development. Our commitment will be to help affected families get their lives back on track, create new opportunities, and further strengthen Nepal’s capacity to deal with future disasters,” he said.PM Modi also highlighted the shared religious and cultural ties between the two countries, referring to the launch of the train service connecting Ayodhya and Janakpur.“Lord Ram and Mata Sita are symbols of our shared civilisation and faith. In 2018, on the sacred land of Janakpur, I had said that our pilgrimage sites are incomplete without Nepal, and our Lord Ram is incomplete without Nepal. In 2024, the consecration ceremony of Ram Lalla took place in Ayodhya. This historic occasion gave renewed strength to our shared faith…With the launch of the Sarayu-Kamala Express train service today, we are giving a new dimension to this sacred bond,” he said.He said India had maintained supplies of fuel and other essential goods to Nepal despite serious challenges related to oil supplies this year, and expressed confidence in the future of bilateral ties.“We will together write a golden chapter of India-Nepal relations,” PM Modi said.The Saryu-Kamala Express will connect Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh with Janakpur Dham in Nepal, covering around 604 km in approximately 19 hours. The regular service will operate once a week in each direction from November 28, enabling pilgrims to travel between the two religious destinations without changing trains.The inaugural run on Monday operated as a special train (No. 04295), departing from Ayodhya Dham at 12.30 pm.The eight MoUs exchanged after the delegation-level talks cover satellite communication, policing, forensic sciences, civil service training, healthcare, traditional medicine, sustainable urban development, and livestock and fisheries development.In the space and communication sector, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and Nepal’s Ministry of Information and Communication signed an MoU to establish a Satellite Communication (SATCOM) Network for the utilisation of the South Asia Satellite.Two agreements aim to strengthen cooperation in policing and forensic sciences. One provides for academic and research collaboration between the National Forensic Sciences University in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, and the Crime Investigation Department of Nepal Police. The other was signed between India’s Rashtriya Raksha University and Nepal’s National Police Academy.For capacity building in public administration, the National Centre for Good Governance, under India’s Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, signed an MoU with Nepal’s Administrative Staff College under the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration. The agreement provides for training programmes for Nepalese civil servants.In healthcare, India’s Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and Nepal’s Ministry of Health and Food Safety signed an MoU on cooperation in health and medicine. The two sides also signed a government-to-government agreement on cooperation in Ayurveda and other traditional systems of medicine.The remaining two agreements provide for technical cooperation in sustainable urban development and collaboration in livestock and fisheries development.At the joint press conference, Balen Shah described India-Nepal relations as being founded on mutual respect, trust and goodwill.“Ties between India and Nepal stand as firm as the Himalayas and as vast as oceans,” he said.He expressed confidence that the agreements and initiatives announced during the visit would take bilateral relations to a new level, while stressing the need for cooperation on climate change.“I am confident that these historic milestones will elevate Nepal-India relations to new heights. The need of the hour is to build on the strong foundation of this enduring relationship and lay solid pillars for the future. Our Himalayas, the sources of clean water, sustain millions across this region. The pristine rivers flowing from the Himalayas into the Ganga remind us of our future and destiny, underscoring the need to address the challenges of climate change through collective action. Nepal and India have been bound by historical, cultural and civilisational ties since the sacred era of Lord Ram and Mata Janaki,” Balen Shah said.Balen Shah arrived in New Delhi on Sunday for a two-day state visit, his first to India since assuming office in March 2026.On Monday, PM Modi received him at Hyderabad House for the bilateral talks. Before the meeting, Shah was accorded a ceremonial welcome at Rashtrapati Bhavan and paid floral tributes to Mahatma Gandhi at the Raj Ghat memorial.Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in a post on X that the leaders would discuss various aspects of bilateral relations and explore new avenues to deepen cooperation.Jaiswal described the ceremonial welcome as reflecting “the special warmth and enduring friendship between India and Nepal” and Shah’s visit to Raj Ghat as “A tribute to the timeless legacy of Mahatma!”
Article Summary: India and Nepal signed eight agreements to expand cooperation in sectors including space technology, security, healthcare, agriculture and sustainable urban development. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah virtually flagged off the Saryu-Kamala Express, connecting Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh with Janakpur in Nepal.

NEW DELHI: The renewed alliance between the Bharatiya Janata Party ( BJP ) and the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) ahead of the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections drew sharp reactions from opposition leaders on Tuesday. Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convenor Arvind Kejriwal accused the two parties of coming together for power and the Congress calling the tie-up opportunistic.The criticism came after Union home minister Amit Shah, BJP president Nitin Nabin and SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal formally announced the alliance at the BJP headquarters in New Delhi. Shah said the two parties would contest all 117 Assembly seats in Punjab, ahead of the 2027 assembly elections, with the SAD to get the chief minister's post.Addressing a joint press conference, Shah said the two parties had decided to fight the Punjab elections together and confirmed that the SAD would rejoin the NDA.“Both the BJP and the Akali Dal have decided to fight the Punjab Assembly elections together and the Akali Dal will also join the NDA from today. This is a great occasion that on Guru Purab the Akali Dal, one of our oldest allies is returning to the NDA,” Shah said.Reacting to the announcement, Kejriwal said the BJP and SAD had repeatedly joined hands and parted ways for political convenience.“Our alliance is with the mothers and daughters of Punjab. Our alliance is with the SC community of Punjab.Our alliance is with the farmers of Punjab. Our alliance is with the traders of Punjab,” Kejriwal said, alleging that political parties come together for power, part ways and reunite.“These people come together for the sake of power, then part ways, and then come together again. We, on the other hand, are working for the development of Punjab. All of Punjab can see how, over the past five years, Bhagwant Mann has worked diligently to try and set things right, to repair the damage inflicted upon Punjab over the last 70–75 years,” he said.“When we spoke to the PM about the expansion of the NDA, he called Sukhbir Badal and said that the NDA is now complete. The Akali Dal and the BJP have a long relationship and this alliance is a symbol of brotherhood and we will move forward together,” Shah said, while announcing the alliance on Tuesday.Meanwhile, Punjab Congress president Pargat Singh termed the alliance a “directionless” tie-up, alleging that the two parties had reunited out of “greed” for power and lacked an agenda for Punjab's development.Reacting to the announcement, Singh told PTI, “The reunion between the SAD and the BJP is only for the greed for power.”“They have no development agenda for Punjab or roadmap for the state's progress. They have joined hands merely for their own development. They have joined hands again with a single motive to capture power in Punjab,” he said, asserting that neither party stood a chance of forming the next government.Singh also asked Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) chief Sukhbir Singh Badal to explain to the people why he had quit the NDA in 2020.AAP leader Jarnail Singh also criticised the reunion, saying, “Zero plus zero will always remain zero. The Akali Dal and the BJP have no future in Punjab, as the people of the state have overwhelmingly rejected both parties for several reasons.”He said people would not forget how more than 700 farmers lost their lives during the protests against the Centre's farm laws. “They will also never forget the sacrilege of the Guru Granth Sahib during the Akali Dal government,” he said.“These two parties, both discredited in the eyes of the people, cannot succeed by joining hands,” Jarnail Singh added.Earlier, Amarinder Singh Raja Warring had also criticised the proposed alliance before its formal announcement. Warring accused Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) leaders Sukhbir Singh Badal and Harsimrat Kaur Badal of misleading voters over their political ties with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), questioning why the two parties had split in 2020.“Sukhbir Badal and Harsimrat Kaur Badal are trying to fool people. Whenever there was a vote in Parliament on issues such as the Presidential election or the Uniform Civil Code, they would stand with the BJP. But when they came here, they would claim that they had no alliance with the BJP. Why did they break the alliance in the first place?” Warring said.Referring to the Centre's three farm laws, he alleged that the Akali Dal initially supported the legislation before changing its position following protests by farmers.Meanwhile, HM Shah outlined the alliance's priorities, identifying the eradication of drugs and corruption and the strengthening of nationalist forces in Punjab as key goals. He announced a deadline for making the state drug-free.Additionally, “Shah said the BJP and SAD would contest all 117 seats in the Punjab Assembly elections. He also indicated that the chief minister's post would go to the SAD as part of the alliance arrangement.”The BJP and SAD ended their alliance in 2020 after the Akali Dal withdrew from the NDA over the Centre's three farm laws, which were subsequently repealed. The parties contested the 2022 Assembly elections separately.Their electoral fortunes had declined in the years after their split. In 2017, the SAD won 15 seats and the BJP three, while in 2022 the SAD secured three seats and the BJP two. The AAP won 92 seats in 2022.
Article Summary: Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convenor Arvind Kejriwal accused the two parties of coming together for power. Union home minister Amit Shah, BJP president Nitin Nabin and SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal formally announced the alliance at the BJP headquarters in New Delhi.

Article Title: From 'nau-mass da rishta' to bitter rivals and back: How BJP-SAD relations played out over the years
Article Text:
How BJP-SAD relations played out over the years

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) have come a long way from describing their partnership as "nau-mass da rishta", a bond as inseparable as nail and skin, to parting ways over the farm laws in 2020.Six years later, the two former allies are back together, reviving a political relationship that has shaped Punjab's electoral landscape for decades.The two parties announced their alliance for the upcoming assembly elections on Tuesday, bringing an end to years of political estrangement.During a press conference, Union home minister Amit Shah said that the two parties would jointly contest all 117 seats, with the Akali Dal taking the lead in the alliance.Shah said extensive discussions had taken place over the past three months between BJP leader Nitin Nabin and SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal on issues concerning Punjab."Over the past three months, extensive discussions have taken place between Nitin Nabin and Sukhbir Singh Badal regarding the challenges faced by Punjab’s farmers, concerns over the state’s economic development, and the employment issues confronting its youth," Shah said.He added that the discussions had resulted in the preparation of a roadmap that would guide the proposed NDA government in the state."These deliberations have culminated in a roadmap, which will serve as the guiding framework for the NDA government that we intend to form," he said.This comes six years after the SAD walked out of the NDA in September 2020 over the Centre's three farm laws, which were subsequently repealed.The BJP and the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) have governed Punjab together for 15 years across three five-year terms. However, their political association goes back even further, predating the formation of the BJP.The Bharatiya Jana Sangh, the BJP's predecessor, was part of the Akali-led government in 1967 and 1969, following the reorganisation of Punjab.The alliance in its present form took shape in 1996, when the SAD, through its Moga Declaration, sought to expand its appeal beyond its traditional Panthic constituency by embracing the idea of "Punjab, Punjabi and Punjabiyat".Coming in the aftermath of militancy in Punjab, the partnership brought together the Akalis' predominantly rural Sikh support base and the BJP's largely urban Hindu constituency. Akali Dal stalwart Parkash Singh Badal used to describe the SAD-BJP tie-up as "nau-mass da rishta" - like nail and skin.Under their longstanding seat-sharing arrangement, the SAD contested 94 of Punjab's 117 assembly seats, leaving 23 for the BJP. In Lok Sabha elections, the parties contested 10 and three seats, respectively. The alliance won 93 seats in the 1997 assembly elections, with the SAD winning 75 and the BJP 18.After losing power to the Congress in 2002, the alliance returned to office in 2007 with 68 seats and retained power in 2012 with an identical tally, bucking Punjab's trend of voting out incumbent governments. However, the emergence of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), along with public anger over incidents of sacrilege and the drug menace, dealt a major blow to the alliance in 2017. The SAD was reduced to 15 seats and the BJP to three.Three years later, the farmers' agitation against the Centre's agricultural reform measures brought the differences between the two parties to a head. On September 17, 2020, Harsimrat Kaur Badal resigned as Union food processing industries minister. Nine days later, the SAD ended its 24-year-old electoral alliance with the BJP.Sukhbir Badal attributed the deterioration in ties to the BJP's growing numerical strength in Parliament, accusing it of not taking its allies into confidence on major policy decisions.However, the repeal of the farm laws in November 2021 did not immediately lead to a rapprochement. In the years that followed, the Akalis accused the BJP of interfering in Sikh religious affairs, even as several senior SAD leaders crossed over to the saffron party.The BJP, meanwhile, sought to shed its image as the junior partner. Its leaders argued that the alliance had constrained the party's organisational expansion in rural Punjab.In the 2022 assembly elections, the SAD, which contested in alliance with the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), won just three seats, with its vote share falling from 25.24 per cent in 2017 to 18.38 per cent. The BJP, which tied up with Amarinder Singh's Punjab Lok Congress and Sukhdev Singh Dhindsa-led SAD (Sanyukt), won two seats. The AAP swept the polls, securing 92 seats.Efforts to revive the alliance ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections failed amid renewed farmers' protests. BJP's vote share in Punjab rose from 9.63 per cent to 18.56 per cent as it contested all 13 seats, while the SAD's share fell from 27.45 per cent to 13.42 per cent. BJP failed to win a single seat, while the SAD retained Bathinda. Their combined vote share of nearly 32 per cent, however, was higher than that of either the Congress or the AAP, strengthening the case for a revival of the alliance.On August 7 this year, speculation about a possible alliance began after Sukhbir Badal met Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Parliament House. PM Modi reached out to Badal's wife and SAD MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal to enquire about the health of Sukhbir Badal after he was attacked at a gurudwara in Maharashtra’s Nanded in AugustHarsimrat Kaur Badal, whose resignation had set the separation in motion, publicly recalled the developmental benefits of the alliance. Her brother and senior SAD leader Bikram Singh Majithia also backed a reunion.
Article Summary: The BJP and the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) have governed Punjab together for 15 years across three five-year terms. The two parties announced their alliance for the upcoming assembly elections on Tuesday. This comes six years after the SAD walked out of the NDA in September 2020 over the Centre's three farm laws, which were subsequently repealed.

Preliminary reports indicated that he had been walking past the restaurant when the explosion occurred.The Independent reported that local residents helped pull the bodies of victims from beneath the rubble. Authorities were concerned that more people could be trapped, as the restaurant was open when the blast struck.Police were using detection equipment to search for survivors and hydraulic machinery to lift concrete slabs. Article Title: US deportee, MBA, BTech graduate: India-America drug probe uncovers unusual profiles

NEW DELHI: A man deported from the US in a drug-related case, an MBA graduate with pharmacy business links and a BTech degree-holder are among the six Indians arrested in a joint India-US investigation into a cross-border drug trafficking network, news agency PTI reported.The probe, conducted by the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) and the US drug enforcement administration (DEA), has been expanded to examine the accused's alleged links and illegal dealings.The six were arrested following multi-city raids conducted between November 4 and 13. Investigators are questioning them about their connections in India and abroad, PTI reported citing officials.One of the accused, T Manoj, 27, from Telangana, was deported from the US in January 2024 for allegedly trading regulated drugs. He holds a BTech degree in Computer Science and was pursuing a master's degree in the US. Investigators are examining his links in both countries.Another accused, TD Jaiswal, 30, from Lucknow, holds an MBA degree and has business links with a pharmacy and a clothing store in the Uttar Pradesh capital.The other accused also have varied educational and professional backgrounds. Arti Soni, 32, from Lucknow, is a Mathematics graduate who worked in corporate event management.A Muttalib, 28, from Kolkata, holds an engineering degree and was engaged in cloth manufacturing and the dairy business.DK Tiwari, 39, an arts graduate, allegedly has business links with Jaiswal, while Jaswant, 29, studied up to Class 12 and worked as an electrician in Lucknow, officials said.The investigation centres on an alleged transnational network that shipped opioid medicines, including Xanax (Alprazolam), Ativan, Tramadol, Valium (Diazepam) and Ambien, from India to customers in the US.The NCB and DEA jointly busted the network in an operation codenamed "Monsoon Thunder".In a statement on November 20, the NCB said records and digital evidence examined so far indicate that the network handled close to 3,000 parcels containing nearly five lakh tablets across the US between June 2022 and November 2026.The agency also shared customer databases covering more than 59,000 subjects with the DEA. These include transaction records, details of past consignments, delivery addresses, USPS tracking IDs and drug types to help identify customers and drop-shippers operating in the US.According to the NCB, Indian operators received drug orders through online platforms such as Telegram, Skype and WhatsApp. The consignments were dispatched through postal and other delivery channels, including the United States Postal Service (USPS).Payments were allegedly routed through digital platforms such as Venmo, bank accounts held in other persons' names, UPI and cryptocurrency, the agency said.

Article Title: 'Once you have power, you may find excuses to keep it': Sonia Gandhi on turning down PM post

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Sonia Gandhi has said she felt the "pull of power" while deciding on whether she should take up the prime ministership in 2004, as she thought that she owed it to party workers who had rallied across the country during the election campaign to accept the post.She said it was a lesson about power that "once you have it, you may find excuses to keep it".The observations came during a conversation with her son Rahul Gandhi and daughter Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, a video of which was shared by them on social media platforms.In the video shared days after the launch of Sonia Gandhi's memoir 'Belonging: A Journey Of Love', the three are seen reminiscing about moments of joy, laughter and pain they felt at various points in time.In a post on X, Rahul Gandhi shared the video and said, "Ma's journey of Belonging has been full of enormous love and terrible tragedy, and she has met all of it with dignity and courage."In the video, Sonia Gandhi talks in detail about the internal conflict she faced while deciding whether to take up the prime minister's post after the Congress-led UPA's victory in the 2004 Lok Sabha elections. She asserts that she did not want power.Talking about the time, Rahul Gandhi says there was a situation unfolding and "we were witnessing the situation from the inside"."On the one hand there was mum saying maybe, maybe not. On the other side there were seven people. There is one gentleman over there who is the best possible PM," he recalls, referring to Manmohan Singh ."The interesting thing is there is only one man who can be PM because of his qualities, capabilities, and there are six-seven dreamers who cannot be. Then my mother decides - 'No (not taking up premiership)'; there is actually joy in the room," he says.Sonia Gandhi says there was another factor playing in her mind that can be called "the pull of power"."You may interpret it like that. But in a way I felt that I owed it to the people, especially the workers who throughout the country had rallied around to vote for the Congress. Since I was leading the campaign, I felt something towards them," she says"How can I let them down and say, 'Bye, I am going'. So that was also part of my thinking. Maybe it was something I wanted to believe for my saying yes," she says, adding that she was analysing her decision in retrospect.She says the experience offered a lesson about power: once one has it, they may find excuses to keep it."I did feel the sense of betrayal that I was betraying all those workers who had rallied around, come sun, come rain, food, or no food, to vote for the Congress," she says.After deliberating, Sonia Gandhi declined to become prime minister following the 2004 poll win and chose Manmohan Singh for the post.Priyanka Gandhi notes that Sonia changed drastically after Rajiv Gandhi entered politics and especially after his assassination.Rahul expresses disgust over the harsh personal attacks, abuse, and hostility Sonia Gandhi faced in Indian politics despite her quiet efforts to assimilate into Indian culture.Sonia Gandhi also recalled an incident during an opposition tour in Bihar when Rajiv Gandhi travelled in an open jeep, and stones were thrown at him amid inadequate security under an opposition state government.Rahul Gandhi alleged that Rajiv Gandhi's security was deliberately withdrawn to create circumstances for his assassination.Sharing the video on X, Sonia Gandhi said, "I wrote Belonging from my memories. Rahul and Priyanka added theirs, and the stories took on a whole new life.""My children are my greatest joy, my strength, and the two people who test my patience like nobody else can," she said.'Belonging: A Journey of Love", officially launched at a packed event at ITC Maurya here last week, was attended by the who's who of the Congress and the INDIA opposition bloc, literary figures and a host of chief ministers, including Tamil Nadu's C Joseph Vijay.
Article Summary: Sonia Gandhi says she felt the "pull of power" while deciding whether to take up the prime ministership in 2004. Article Title: Global South bears brunt of distant wars, India warns UNSC citing Bengal famine
Article Text:
New York, Aug 26 (ANI): India's Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Parvathaneni Harish (Photo: ANI).

NEW DELHI: India has invoked the devastating Bengal famine of 1943 at the UN Security Council , warning that the economic and humanitarian fallout of global conflicts is borne disproportionately by countries of the Global South.Speaking at a high-level briefing on protecting critical energy infrastructure and Black Sea food supply routes on Monday, India’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, said the food, fuel and fertiliser crisis triggered by conflicts was hitting developing nations hardest.“India has consistently emphasised that the costs of conflict are not shared equally,” Parvathaneni said, adding that Global South countries were among those most adversely affected by disruptions caused by wars.Drawing a parallel with World War II, he said the Bengal famine, which killed more than three million people, remained a stark reminder of how people far removed from the battlefield could suffer the consequences of distant conflicts and wartime decisions.“The pain and suffering caused by the devastating Bengal famine of 1943 in India that killed over 3 million people in India, is a stark reminder of the terrible human cost of a distant conflict caused by unchecked wartime priorities and calculations,” he said.The Ukraine conflict, now in its fifth year, has disrupted interconnected supply chains, with consequences extending far beyond the region, Parvathaneni said. Recalling Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for the world to move from “endless war to the end of war”, he said India remained ready to contribute to efforts for a peaceful resolution.India said conflicts deepen food insecurity by disrupting farming, displacing communities, damaging infrastructure and restricting humanitarian access. Their impact spreads through energy and fertiliser supplies, transport networks and agricultural trade, with the Global South bearing a disproportionate burden.“For the Global South, peace is not in the abstract. It is achieved when hungry mouths are fed, when a ship reaches a port, and when a seafarer returns home safe,” Parvathaneni said.India also urged the Security Council to prioritise humanitarian access, protect civilian infrastructure and ensure freedom of navigation, so that humanitarian supplies and legitimate trade could continue without disruption.Parvathaneni said the Black Sea region and India together account for nearly a fifth of global cereal production, while Russia and Ukraine account for almost a quarter of global exports of wheat, maize and barley.He said the importance of the region to global food security showed how disruptions to agricultural production and maritime connectivity could have consequences worldwide.India also highlighted its humanitarian assistance, including wheat supplies to Afghanistan, rice to Sudan and aid to Palestine, as part of its efforts to support global food security.Parvathaneni expressed concern over attacks on merchant vessels and their crews in conflict zones, noting that Indian seafarers had lost their lives in such incidents.“We call for an end to the targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers, and for safe navigation through international waterways to be restored at the earliest,” he said.India and Liberia launched the Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers during the UN high-level week in September. Parvathaneni said India was also engaging directly with both sides on shipping safety and grain corridors, while supporting the work of the International Maritime Organisation and the International Labour Organisation.
Article Summary: Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni said the food, fuel and fertiliser crisis triggered by conflicts was hitting developing nations hardest. He said the Bengal famine, which killed more than three million people, remained a stark reminder of how people far removed from the battlefield could suffer the consequences of distant conflicts.

NEW DELHI: Six years after parting ways, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) on Tuesday announced the revival of their alliance for the 2027 Punjab assembly elections , setting the stage for a potentially three-cornered contest against the ruling Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and the Congress.The announcement, made on Gurpurab , comes with a symbolic connection to the events that led to the breakdown of the alliance.Union home minister Amit Shah opened the joint press conference by extending Gurpurab greetings and describing the gathering as an "NDA ki press vaarta". Shiromani Akali Dal chief Sukhbir Singh Badal and BJP president Nitin Nabin were also present at the press conference at the BJP headquarters in New Delhi."From today onwards, the Akali Dal will work in politics as an officially recognised ally of the NDA. He expressed the sentiment that the NDA is now complete," Shah said.The return of the BJP-SAD combine could reshape the electoral contest in Punjab, where both parties have struggled to regain their earlier political strength. Their combined performance in the 2022 assembly elections was significantly weaker than their showing during their years in power.The BJP-SAD alliance has been revived six years after the two parties parted ways over the contentious farm laws, which had triggered widespread protests by farmers.In a symbolic coincidence, Prime Minister Narendra Modi had announced the repeal of the three farm laws on Gurpurab, November 19, 2021. The alliance has now been stitched together again on the occasion of Gurpurab.The SAD-BJP alliance enjoyed its strongest electoral run in 2007 and 2012, when the Akali Dal retained power in Punjab for two consecutive terms. The BJP, meanwhile, saw its tally drop from 19 seats in 2007 to just 2 in 2022, a decline of nearly 89%.The Congress also witnessed a sharp reversal in its electoral fortunes. After winning 77 seats and forming the government in 2017, it was reduced to 18 seats in the 2022 elections.The AAP, meanwhile, emerged as the dominant force in the state, winning 92 of the 117 assembly seats in 2022 and forming the government under Bhagwant Mann.The renewed alliance will seek to combine the BJP's support among Hindu voters with the SAD's traditional Panthic base among sections of the Sikh electorate.
